items.headline: Review Analyzes How Cancer Immunotherapies Trigger Thrombosis and Shape Anticoagulation Strategies
items.preview: A review in Biomarker Research explores the link between cancer immunotherapies and thrombosis.
items.article:
A comprehensive scientific review published in Biomarker Research evaluates the complex relationship between antitumor immunity and vascular complications, detailing how cancer immunotherapies trigger thrombosis and alter systemic coagulation pathways.
Why this matters: The authors emphasize that while these treatments provide revolutionary breakthroughs in tumor control, the vascular risks they pose demand precise mechanistic differentiation and carefully balanced management strategies.
Clinical investigations demonstrate that immune checkpoint inhibitors constitute an independent risk factor for thromboembolic events, with cumulative venous thromboembolism incidence reaching approximately 7.13 percent to 7.6 percent at six months. Furthermore, combination regimens exacerbate this risk compared to single-agent therapies.
The review also discusses the distinct clinical syndromes associated with CAR-T therapy and highlights the need for developing dynamic risk scoring frameworks to manage thrombosis in patients undergoing immunotherapy.

items.headline: Nose drops could offer world-first non-invasive delivery system for Alzheimer’s drugs
items.preview: Researchers at the University of Sydney have developed nose drops that could treat Alzheimer’s disease.
items.article:
Inspired by science fiction, researchers have designed nose drops that protect against cognitive decline in mice and could offer a revolutionary delivery system to treat Alzheimer’s disease.
Why this matters: If successful in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer’s that bypasses the blood–brain barrier.
The study shows that delivering mRNA packaged in lipid nanoparticles can enhance learning and memory in aged mice while preventing memory loss in a mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease. The findings suggest that this method could support neuron health and connectivity without clearing amyloid plaques, potentially complementing existing therapies.

items.headline: EVerZom leads €13.3M EU project to test extracellular vesicles where Takeda failed
items.preview: EVerZom is leading a €13.3 million EU project to develop an extracellular vesicle therapy for Crohn’s disease.
items.article:
French biotech EVerZom is leading a consortium that has secured €13.3 million in EU funding to bring its extracellular vesicle-based therapy for Crohn’s disease-associated perianal fistulas into clinical trials.
Why this matters: EVerZom aims to overcome limitations of previous cell therapies by using biological material secreted by cells rather than the cells themselves.
The project will include a first-in-human Phase 1b/2a trial and a subsequent Phase 2b trial, focusing on safety, tolerability, and preliminary efficacy measures. EVerZom's approach promises advantages such as stability, consistency, and local retention of therapeutic agents.

items.headline: Contera spins out RNA drug company Threepoint, opening door to outside investment
items.preview: Contera Pharma has spun out its RNA drug business as Threepoint Therapeutics, seeking outside investment.
items.article:
Denmark-based Contera Pharma has spun out its RNA drug business as Threepoint Therapeutics, which is now open to outside investment as it grows.
Why this matters: The spin-out allows Threepoint to focus on RNA drug development, which has matured significantly, while Contera continues its work on Parkinson’s disease.
Threepoint's lead program targets Canavan disease with an antisense oligonucleotide designed to normalize N-acetylaspartate levels in the brain. The company aims to expand its pipeline and establish strategic partnerships for future growth.

items.headline: Periodontal Disease Is Modestly Associated With Increased Breast Cancer Risk
items.preview: A review in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology links periodontal disease to breast cancer risk.
items.article:
A comprehensive narrative review published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology evaluates the relationship between chronic periodontal disease and breast cancer incidence.
Why this matters: The review outlines how chronic inflammatory breakdown of periodontal tissues corresponds to a modest increase in breast cancer risk among adults.
Epidemiological evidence indicates that individuals with periodontal disease have a higher hazard of developing breast cancer, with various studies showing adjusted hazard ratios indicating a positive association. The review also discusses the bidirectional relationship, where cancer treatments can lead to declines in periodontal health, creating a detrimental cycle.
